extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (authors, lecturers) preparing expository mathematics: papers, books, lectures, and notes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, honest, and well-organized mathematical exposition (theorems, proofs, definitions, lectures, and papers), with rules about honesty, notation, wording, repetition, and finishing. Applies to authors preparing manuscripts and lectures in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete honesty about status of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader the status of every assertion: what has been proved, what hasn't, what will be proved later, and what you don't know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you claim a non-implication (p does not imply q) make clear whether it is obvious, whether a counterexample will be supplied later, whether it is a standard but irrelevant fact (give a reference), or whether you simply tried and failed to derive q (confess). Avoid giving the reader the impression that you know more than you do. When you call something 'obvious' or 'easy to see', ensure you really believe it, have let the manuscript 'ripen', explained it to others, and confirmed it isn't false—the major rule being: make sure the 'obvious' is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant and trivial assumptions (theorem statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit irrelevant hypotheses and treat trivial cases explicitly; state theorems early, clearly, and succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce assumptions that distract (e.g. 'commutative semisimple ring with unit' when irrelevant). Explicitly mention or exclude trivial cases (e.g. behavior at 0). State the theorem before long rambling text: give preliminaries and motivation first, then the statement, then the proof. Keep the statement to one (short) sentence whenever possible; avoid 'chit-chat' inside theorem statements. If many hypotheses/conclusions are present, check whether they belong in a single theorem or should be isolated as a general concept deserving its own name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition deliberately; avoid needless repetition and repeating proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ word-for-word repetition to emphasize parallel structure, but avoid restating the same content in different words or redoing proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good repetition: reuse identical phrasing for parallel constructions so differences stand out, and rewrite earlier sections to create helpful parallelism. Bad repetition: rephrasing the same idea unnecessarily (which confuses the reader) and repeating proofs verbatim. If proofs are similar, introduce a lemma that both theorems use rather than copying the argument; avoid signals like 'by the same technique' without isolating the common lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the editorial 'we' and pronouns sensibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer neutral, unobtrusive style; avoid overusing 'I' or the pompous 'one'; use 'we' to mean author+reader when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple declarative sentences with minimal pronouns ('Since p, it follows that q.'). Imperative forms are effective ('Given p, put q equal to r.'). Let 'we' mean the author and the reader (e.g. 'Using Lemma 2 we can...') but do not misuse it for personal history ('Our work was done in 1969') or trivial social remarks ('We thank our wife...'). Use 'I' only in short notes, personal remarks, or when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words correctly (logical and common words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words with care—logical connectives and common words can change mathematical meaning; avoid ambiguous words like 'any' and sloppy uses like 'equivalent' for informal relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'any' in mathematical writing; prefer 'each' or 'every' or recast the sentence. Avoid 'where' as lazy afterthought; avoid using 'equivalent' loosely to mean 'related by similar difficulty'. Recast nested 'if... then... if... then' constructions to improve readability. Think about small words (where, if, then, equivalent) because they affect logic and reader psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms correctly and consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard mathematical terms precisely (e.g., distinguish functions from their values; 'sequence' means a function on naturals) and maintain terminological consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating unnecessary new technical terms; when you must, choose them carefully. Examples: don't say 'the function z^2+1 is even' — say 'the function f defined by f(z)=z^2+1 is even' or 'z↦z^2+1'. Use 'sequence' only when domain=N; use 'countable set' when appropriate. Consistency in language, notation, references, and typography reduces irritation and misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist overuse of symbols and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer prose where possible; avoid superfluous symbols, free variables, labels, and overly symbolic or machine-style presentations that impede human understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best notation is minimal notation. Avoid irrelevant symbols in statements (e.g. naming a function f when it adds nothing), avoid introducing a symbol only to use it once, and avoid gratuitous labels for displays. In induction and similar arguments, a short exemplary case plus 'and so on' may be clearer than heavy symbolic detail. Write proofs 'forward' for the human reader rather than backward machine-checkable versions. Replace chains of equations with explanatory prose of the steps ('first substitute p for q, then collect terms...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and punctuation correctly and consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate symbols into consistent verbal forms, punctuate symbolic clauses as you would sentences, and avoid starting sentences with symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on a verbal reading (e.g. read '∈' as 'is in' and use it consistently: 'If x ∈ A, then x ∈ B'). Punctuate mathematical clauses like ordinary clauses; don't overwork commas or periods near symbols. Avoid starting sentences with a bare symbol—use a word in apposition ('The set X belongs...'). Keep the verbal translation of a symbol consistent across the text, and consider layout (balance of prose and displays) so pages are readable (not too dense prose or too many displays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt exposition to medium: all communication is exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Books, articles, lectures, and letters share the same expository principles, but adjust for differences of medium (e.g., audience attention span, blackboard growth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lecture demands more omission and fewer computations than a paper (hearers have shorter attention spans and cannot backtrack). The blackboard allows building ideas dynamically; don't fill it before starting. The same content planning (content, aim, organization, grammar, diction, notation) applies to all media—adjust detail and pacing to medium-specific constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend your stylistic choices against mechanical copyediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to argue for consistent, meaningful stylistic or typographical choices when editors or copyreaders apply blanket rules mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial assistants may misapply typographical style rules (e.g., hyphenation, punctuation inside quotes) and introduce nonsense ('nonmeasure preserving transformation') by mechanical edits. Authors should be ready to explain why punctuation or hyphens belong where they do and to insist on logical placement of commas/periods relative to quotations and mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop (finish ruthlessly)
rubrics_metrics.description: After proofreading, checking computations, and letting the manuscript ripen, stop polishing—be ruthless and finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There will always be something left undone; use proofreading, ripening (putting manuscript away for months), and a quick final read to test major points (is the mathematics good, is exposition interesting, is language clear, is layout pleasant). After these checks, stop rather than endlessly chasing marginal improvements, since further polishing leads to new mirages of improvement.
